title: What If Meetings Were Voluntary?
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Most internal meetings fail to generate enough value that people would willingly attend them, largely because they are structured around status updates and unfocused discussions rather than genuine debate and problem-solving. The best-practice response is pre-work: each agenda item is assigned to a team member who prepares a short written brief framing the issue, and a clear question must be articulated before any topic can be discussed at the meeting. This shift moves meeting time almost entirely into high-quality discussion—the only activity that justifies bringing people together. When discussion and debate dominate, even the most talented team members choose to attend rather than skip, because they know they would miss something consequential. Leaders who make their meetings earn their existence by delivering what no other format can find that their teams show up willingly, not out of obligation.
points: The voluntary-meeting test is a useful diagnostic: if most of your talented people would skip your meetings given the choice, the meetings are not delivering enough value.
Pre-work—short written briefs that frame each issue before the meeting—shifts time from presentation to discussion, which is the only reason to gather people in the first place.
A clear question is the minimum threshold for any agenda item; if a team member can't articulate the question sharply, the issue is tabled.
When discussion and debate dominate a meeting, attendance becomes self-motivated—people show up because they don't want to miss a consequential conversation.
quotes: Many internal meetings don't provide the kind of value that compels people to want to attend.
The truth is that most meetings are boring by design. They're built around status updates and lengthy discussions that don't go anywhere.
Each issue or decision is assigned to a team member, who frames the context in a short written brief that the team can digest before the meeting.
A clear question is the minimum bar for discussing anything at the meeting.
In the best organizations, a meeting earns its existence by doing something that can't be done in other formats or with other tools.
When they know they'd miss a lively debate on an issue or decision that affects them, team members willingly show up — even if they don't have to.
